item.title: Comment on The new tariffs are bad by Naveen_K
item.description:
Everyone will discuss the economics of this, but we should first discuss the laws and premises under which these tariffs are being imposed.

While the Trump administration has not explicitly detailed the specific legal authority for these tariffs, he is likely utilizing powers granted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) of 1977. This act allows the President to regulate commerce during a declared national emergency related to an "unusual and extraordinary threat" to U.S. national security, economy, or foreign policy.

Not a single human being in the US thinks Canada and Mexico pose an "unusual and extraordinary threat" to US national security.

Trump unilaterally imposing tariffs under such blatantly false premises is no better than Biden forgiving student loans under the equally dishonest and false premise of the HEROES Act, which only applies to federal student financial assistance during national emergencies. He forgave student loans long after COVID-19 became an ongoing concern.

Every US President in my adult lifetime has can come into office and has abused executive power on blatantly false premises or exercised power that he previously said he didn't have (Obama on DACA). Trump and Biden unilaterally impose tariffs based on dishonest pretenses of national security. Biden forgives student loans for politically favorable voters on obviously dishonesty pretenses of COVID-19 emergencies. Despite Obama admitting the President doesn't have the power to do so on the record ten times, after reelection, institutes DACA and DAPA.

Thankfully Senator Kaine and Senator Coons have introduced the introduced the Stopping Tariffs on Allies and Bolstering Legislative Exercise of (STABLE) Trade Policy Act. But, of course, it has no chance of being passed as a law. Maybe the party that was shouting Norms! for 4 years and had the VP as the tie-breaking vote should have passed this law before Trump came into office.

I hate everyone.

P.S. Can we take a moment to talk about how low Trump’s verbal IQ is?

“The tariffs are going to make us very rich, and very strong,”
"It's pure economic."

This is the level of English Trump is capable of at all times and in every setting imaginable. It's unbelievable that this buffoon is the President of the United States of America. People, even 15 years from now, will find it hard to believe. (I'd have voted for Trump too).

George Bush was widely mocked for his mistakes while speaking, but he only misspoke occasionally. But this is how Trump talks **all the time***; like a mentally retarded spastic.

item.title: Comment on The new tariffs are bad by So
item.description:
Reply to Sure:

Who exactly had agency on this that we should we be holding responsible otherwise?

Trump clearly believes that these sorts of presidential powers are right and good so it would be inconsistent for him to advocate for legislation to curtail them. At worst, Trump is wrong, but
he is just practicing what he preached during an election where a majority of the voters signed off.

Congressional Republicans were last in a position where they could pass reforms without Democratic support in ... 2006 (and that likely contingent on at least soft acquiescence over the filibuster, getting past that hurdle where Republicans had the votes to also get cloture without Democratic agency was in ... 1928).

Democrats, on the other hand, did not seem to be running on a tariff heavy presidential score in either 2016 or 2020. They had unified control with a presumably amenable president in 2020. In terms of getting past the filibuster, they had the option in 2008.

The critique here is that if this is a violation of norms, then we should have seen something to legislatively protect those norms by folks who had the power to do it. Yet we don't see that. Biden does not even try to get Senate Democrats to pass something to unequivocally reserve this power to Congress in December.

And the reality is that passing this sort of legislation is either going to require a very favorable review from the Senate Parliamentarian, going Harry Reid on some technical aspect of reconciliation or whatever to change Senate norms, or - and most practically - at least tacit bipartisan support.

And this is the reality of Washington. The voters, twice, voted in somebody explicitly running on tariffs. Most recently they did so with an absolute plurality a hair's breadth away from a majority. The only power bloc that might be able to pull the strings here unilaterally - just explicitly campaigned on the exact opposite.

If the goal is protecting republican norms, I would submit that it would be a rather big stretch to save the republic by immediately doing 180 degrees of what you campaigned to do. Voters are sovereign and they are getting what they wanted, perhaps good and hard, and that is the democratic outcome.

On the charge of stupidity, counter productiveness, cruelty, or whatever the Republicans can be easily tarred. Maybe the public will vote on that in 2026. On the charge of hypocrisy, there simply is not a power configuration that could support that in this generation of elected Republicans. On the charge of hypocrisy, there simply was a time where a Democratic coalition that claims unified partisan opposition to this sort of executive power grab very recently.

And that is the difference. On this issue Republicans might be wrong, but consistent. Democrats might be right, but inconsistent. The voters may revise their judgement, but Trump doing what he said he would while campaigning could be many horrible things ... just not hypocrisy.

What on earth are you talking about? The last Republican trifecta was during Trump’s first term.

This is literally the reason stated by Trump for the tariffs. We pretend to be a superpower while our establishment allows anyone and everyone to abuse us as they see fit. It's a humiliation ritual perpetuated by traitorous leftists that enriches the elite class at our expense, but naturally you're more concerned with appearances and keeping up relations with foreigners who don't give a shit about you than acting in the best interests of the nation.

Most major categories of violent and property crime are also still well below their levels in the 90s so allegations that criminals are entering the U.S. also cannot be a serious way to invoke national security.
